# Part II review {#sec-review-2 .unnumbered}

These exercises mix ideas from Parts I and II. They don't say which chapter they come from, so part of each exercise is deciding which method to use. Solutions, with the chapters each exercise draws on, are in [Solutions: Part II](../appendices/solutions-2.qmd#sec-solutions-review-2).

1. []{#exercise-review-2-1}Solve by Gaussian elimination:
   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   x + 2y + z &= 4, \\
   2x + 5y + 3z &= 10, \\
   x + 3y + 4z &= 8.
   \end{aligned}
   $$
   Then use your row echelon form to find the determinant of the coefficient matrix, without expanding it.

   [Solution to exercise 1](../appendices/solutions-2.qmd#solution-review-2-1){.sol-link}

2. []{#exercise-review-2-2}For which values of $a$ and $b$ does the system
   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   x + y + z &= 1, \\
   x + 2y + 3z &= 2, \\
   2x + 3y + az &= b
   \end{aligned}
   $$
   have (i) exactly one solution, (ii) no solution, (iii) infinitely many solutions? In case (iii), find the reduced row echelon form and write down the general solution. What do the three planes look like in each case?

   [Solution to exercise 2](../appendices/solutions-2.qmd#solution-review-2-2){.sol-link}

3. []{#exercise-review-2-3}Find the inverse of
   $$\M{A} = \mat{1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1}$$
   by Gauss–Jordan elimination. Check your answer using the determinant of $\M{A}$, then use the inverse to solve $\M{A}\vect{x} = (1, 1, 1)\T$.

   [Solution to exercise 3](../appendices/solutions-2.qmd#solution-review-2-3){.sol-link}

4. []{#exercise-review-2-4}Find the LU decomposition of
   $$\M{A} = \mat{2 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 & 3 \\ 8 & 7 & 9}$$
   without row swaps. Use it to find $\det\M{A}$, and to solve $\M{A}\vect{x} = (4, 10, 24)\T$ by forward and back substitution.

   [Solution to exercise 4](../appendices/solutions-2.qmd#solution-review-2-4){.sol-link}

5. []{#exercise-review-2-5}Let $\vect{a}_1 = (1, 1, 0)\T$, $\vect{a}_2 = (0, 1, 1)\T$ and $\vect{a}_3 = (1, 2, 1)\T$, and let $\M{A}$ be the matrix with these columns. Find the rank of $\M{A}$. Is $\vect{b} = (1, 0, 1)\T$ a combination of the columns? Is $\vect{b} = (1, 3, 2)\T$? Explain each answer in terms of the rank of the augmented matrix.

   [Solution to exercise 5](../appendices/solutions-2.qmd#solution-review-2-5){.sol-link}

6. []{#exercise-review-2-6}Balance the equation for burning propane,
   $$a\,\mathrm{C_3H_8} + b\,\mathrm{O_2} \to c\,\mathrm{CO_2} + d\,\mathrm{H_2O},$$
   by writing it as a homogeneous linear system and finding the smallest whole-number solution.

   [Solution to exercise 6](../appendices/solutions-2.qmd#solution-review-2-6){.sol-link}

7. []{#exercise-review-2-7}A computer solves a dense $1000 \times 1000$ system by LU decomposition in 0.2 seconds. Roughly how long will it take for a $4000 \times 4000$ system? If you then need to solve 50 more systems with the same $4000 \times 4000$ matrix but different right-hand sides, roughly how much extra time does that take if you keep the LU factors, and how much if you start again each time?

   [Solution to exercise 7](../appendices/solutions-2.qmd#solution-review-2-7){.sol-link}

8. []{#exercise-review-2-8}**Code.** For the matrix in exercise 4, factorise once (with `lu_factor` in Python or `lu` in MATLAB), then solve for the right-hand sides $(4, 10, 24)\T$, $\ue{1}$, $\ue{2}$ and $\ue{3}$. Use the last three solutions to build $\M{A}^{-1}$, and compare it with the built-in inverse.
